analysis.one_liner: Cracks down on unwanted robocalls: tighter definitions, caller ID verification, and easier opt-outs.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 58 cosponsors and a subcommittee hearing but never got a House vote, dying in committee when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the nation's robocall law to cover more automated calls and texts, let people revoke consent to be called in any reasonable way, require a nationwide database of reassigned phone numbers, and force phone companies to verify caller ID information at no extra charge to customers. It would also lengthen the time the government has to punish robocall violators and require annual reports on enforcement. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, held one subcommittee hearing, and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with a phone, especially people bombarded by scam and telemarketing robocalls. The bill expands what counts as an unlawful robocall to cover modern dialing equipment and texts, lets consumers stop calls in any reasonable way, requires a database so callers can't claim they thought a reassigned number was still the old customer's, mandates caller ID authentication technology so spoofed calls can be blocked, bars phone companies from charging subscribers for it, and gives the FCC longer to pursue violators.

how_it_helps.text: Expands the definition of 'robocall' to cover calls made with equipment that dials stored or generated numbers, closing loopholes around modern auto-dialers, and includes text messages.
Lets consumers revoke prior consent to be called at any time and in any reasonable manner, regardless of how they originally agreed to be called.
Requires a nationwide, up-to-date database of reassigned phone numbers so callers cannot use a number's reassignment as an excuse, while giving compliant callers a safe harbor from liability.

Directs the FCC to require voice providers to implement caller ID authentication that verifies call information and blocks unverified calls, and prohibits providers from charging subscribers extra for it.
Removes the requirement of an FCC citation before seeking forfeiture penalties and extends the statute of limitations for robocall and caller ID violations from two to four years.

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketers, call centers, and other high-volume callers would face a broader definition of illegal robocalls, tighter limits on exemptions, easier revocation of consent, a reassigned-number database that undercuts the 'wrong number' defense, and a longer window for penalties. Phone and VoIP providers would bear the cost of building caller ID authentication and reporting number reassignments, and could not bill subscribers for the authentication technology.
analysis.who_pays_short: Telemarketers, call centers, and phone carriers

drawbacks.text: The bill gives callers who check the reassigned-number database a broad safe harbor from liability, so some calls made to reassigned numbers would escape penalties even when a consumer gets an unwanted call.

Phone and VoIP providers would bear the cost of implementing caller ID authentication technology and database reporting; while the bill bans charging subscribers extra, those compliance costs could still pressure prices elsewhere.

Callers relying on exemptions, such as certain healthcare, utility, or informational callers, would face new conditions on who they can call, how often, and with what opt-out mechanisms, adding compliance burden to some legitimate callers.
The bill relies on FCC rulemaking with one-year deadlines, so real protection would depend on the commission writing and enforcing detailed regulations after enactment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefits are large and concrete: fewer scam and spoofed calls, easier opt-outs, and stronger enforcement, aimed at a problem that touches nearly every phone user. The main costs fall on the telemarketing and calling industry, which is the point, plus real but manageable compliance costs for phone providers. The safe harbor is a genuine carve-out, but it is conditioned on callers actually checking the database. On balance, the bill is a well-targeted consumer protection measure.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee, got a single subcommittee hearing in April 2019, and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 4, 2019, with 17 original cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
It was referred the next day to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology, which held a hearing on April 30, 2019.
The bill gathered 58 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, but the full committee never marked it up and the House never voted on it.
Its only committee action was one subcommittee hearing; the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-volume robocallers and telemarketers kept operating under the old, narrower rules for the rest of the Congress, and phone carriers avoided the mandated caller ID authentication and database-reporting obligations this bill would have imposed. Congress did later enact a related robocall law in the same Congress (the TRACED Act), so some of the substance was delivered through a different bill, but this bill itself died without a vote.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 17 original cosponsors.

for.name: 58 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans signed on.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought H.R. 946 to the floor; the House instead considered a later, broader robocall bill in December 2019.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes on the bill, so no roll-call split exists; all 58 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republicans signed on, while the bill died quietly in committee rather than being voted down.

industries.note: The bill's broadened definition of robocall, easier consent revocation, reassigned-number database, and longer enforcement window would directly cut into the business of mass automated calling. Its loss was a gain for operations that profit from high-volume calling to consumers.

Providers would have to implement caller ID authentication and report number reassignments at their own cost, but could not charge subscribers extra, and would gain a safe harbor from liability if they use the reassigned-number database. Avoiding these mandates while the bill died modestly benefited carriers.

industries.industry: Businesses that call customers with prior consent (debt collection, healthcare reminders, utilities)
industries.note: Consent-based callers would face new limits on call volume, purposes, and mandatory opt-out mechanisms, but also gain clarity and a safe harbor through the reassigned-number database that reduces lawsuits over calls to reassigned numbers.
